# gpsd-tools

**cgps and gpsmon — the two programs you actually reach for when a receiver misbehaves**

- **Version recorded:** 3.25
- **Categories:** `hardware`, `station`, `timing`
- **Upstream:** <https://gpsd.io/>
- **Needs first:** `gpsd`

## What it does

Three terminal programs: `cgps`, a live fix and satellite display; `gpsmon`, which shows the raw sentences the receiver is sending; and `gpssnmp`, which exposes fix and satellite data as SNMP OIDs so an ordinary network monitoring system can watch a receiver.

## Why you would want it

The first question about a misbehaving receiver is always whether it has a fix at all, and `cgps` answers it in one command with no X server and no scripting. `gpsmon` answers the second question — whether the receiver is saying anything — which matters because a receiver with a dead antenna and a receiver on the wrong baud rate look identical from any higher level.

## Before it will work

gpsd running. This is a separate package from `gpsd-clients` on Debian, which is worth knowing before spending an evening wondering where `cgps` went.

## How it installs

- apt: `gpsd-tools`

## Known problems

`gpsmon` can switch a receiver between NMEA and binary mode — its own manual documents the mode-toggling commands and warns about switching dual-protocol units (gpsmon(1), gpsd 3.25, Debian 13) — so run one tool at a time rather than gpsmon and cgps against the same device.
